meta.title: Who really said "People often overestimate what will happen in the next two years and underestimate what will happen in ten"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuinely Bill Gates: The Road Ahead, 1996 revised edition, Afterword, p. 316. The idea is older — Quote Investigator traces it to a 1965 anonymous maxim.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'People often overestimate what will happen in the next two years and underestimate what will happen in ten'?
meta.ogDescription: Yes, Gates wrote it — The Road Ahead (1996 revised ed.), Afterword, p. 316. But he did not coin the idea: it was already in print, unattributed, in 1965.

answer.sourceLine: This one is real, and it is unusually well documented. Quote Investigator ↗ cites the sentence to the Afterword of the second, revised edition of Gates’s The Road Ahead (Penguin Books, 1996), quote page 316, where it runs on: “I’m guilty of this myself.” What Gates did not do is invent the thought — the same maxim was already in print, credited to nobody, in 1965.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Second edition, “completely revised and up-to-date” — Penguin Books, 1996 (first published by Viking Penguin, 24 November 1995)

source.excerpt: People often overestimate what will happen in the next two years and underestimate what will happen in ten. I’m guilty of this myself.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ pins the exact wording to a specific place: “1996, The Road Ahead by Bill Gates with Nathan Myhrvold and Peter Rinearson, Second Edition, Section: Afterword, Quote Page 316, Penguin Books, New York.” The sentence it transcribes is the one on this page, followed by “I’m guilty of this myself.”

A second, independent sourced-quotation database agrees. WIST ↗ carries the identical wording and cites it to The Road Ahead, “Afterword” (1996 ed.), noting that similar formulations go back to the 1960s and linking to Quote Investigator for them.

The edition history checks out. Wikipedia’s article on the book ↗ records a Viking Penguin hardback on 24 November 1995 and a Penguin Books paperback in October 1996 billed “completely revised and up-to-date” — the revision prompted by how badly the hardback had underrated the internet, which is exactly what the Afterword sentence is about. The Internet Archive holds a 1996 Penguin printing ↗; we could not read its interior from here, so the page number above rests on Quote Investigator’s citation rather than our own inspection of a scan.

One honest gap: this line is not listed on Wikiquote’s Bill Gates page ↗ in any section — not sourced, not attributed, not misattributed. Its absence there is neither support nor contradiction; the sourcing here comes from Quote Investigator and WIST.
source.excerptNote: As transcribed by Quote Investigator from page 316 of the second edition. The second sentence is almost always dropped when the line is quoted, which turns a self-criticism into a piece of general wisdom.

author.name: Bill Gates
author.heading: Bill Gates
author.metaLine: Born 1955 · Microsoft co-founder, author and philanthropist
author.bio: William Henry Gates III co-founded Microsoft with Paul Allen in 1975 and served as its chief executive for 25 years before moving to chief software architect and, later, stepping back from the company’s day-to-day running. Alongside the software career he became a bestselling business writer: The Road Ahead (1995, revised 1996), Business @ the Speed of Thought (1999), and later books on climate and pandemics. Since the 2000s his principal work has been the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation.

misattribution.heading: What actually gets misattributed here
misattribution.intro: Unusually for a Bill Gates quotation, the wording is his. What gets misattributed is the idea — Gates is constantly credited with coining a maxim he was quoting, and the same thought circulates under at least three other names.

items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ gives the earliest known appearance as J. C. R. Licklider’s Libraries of the Future (MIT Press, 1965), page 17, where it is introduced as “a modern maxim” — Licklider explicitly did not claim it as his own.

The best-known rival form — “We tend to overestimate the effect of a technology in the short run and underestimate the effect in the long run” — carries Roy Amara ↗’s name. But Quote Investigator’s earliest citation linking Amara to the notion is a 1983 Gannett News Service interview, and QI concludes Amara did not originate the saying.

Clarke is often named as the source. Quote Investigator examined the claim and found the evidence linking him to this specific expression weak — his 1951 remark was about daring prophecies coming to seem laughably conservative, a different point. See the QI analysis ↗.

items.who: “We always overestimate the change that will occur in the next two years…”
items.why: That longer variant is real Gates too, but it is not this sentence and not this book: Quote Investigator cites it to Business @ the Speed of Thought (Warner Books, 1999), chapter 4, page 69. It is habitually reprinted as though it came from The Road Ahead ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Bill Gates wrote this exact sentence in the 1996 revised edition of The Road Ahead — about his own failure to see the internet coming. He was restating a maxim that Quote Investigator ↗ finds already in print, credited to no one, in 1965.

context.heading: Why he wrote it
lead: The line is a confession as much as an observation. When The Road Ahead first appeared in hardback in November 1995, published by Viking Penguin, it treated the internet as one precursor among several to the “information highway” Gates expected to arrive. That call aged badly, fast. The following year Penguin Books issued a paperback billed as “completely revised and up-to-date ↗,” rewritten around the internet Gates had underweighted.

The sentence sits in that revised edition’s Afterword, and the clause most people drop is the one that gives it its point. Gates does not offer the maxim as advice for other forecasters; he offers it as the diagnosis of his own error, then adds — per Quote Investigator’s transcription ↗ — “I’m guilty of this myself.”
context.detailsSummary: The older maxim behind the sentence
detailsBody: The shape of the idea is much older than 1996. Quote Investigator’s earliest documented instance is in J. C. R. Licklider ↗’s Libraries of the Future (MIT Press, 1965), page 17 — and Licklider presents it as common property: “A modern maxim says: ‘People tend to overestimate what can be done in one year and to underestimate what can be done in five or ten years.’” Note the different intervals: one year and five-or-ten, not two and ten.

Gates himself returned to the idea in Business @ the Speed of Thought (Warner Books, 1999), chapter 4, page 69, in a looser form: “we always overestimate the change that will occur in the next two years and underestimate the change that will occur in the next ten.” That second phrasing is the one most often quoted online — and it is routinely, and wrongly, filed under The Road Ahead.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator cites the exact wording "People often overestimate what will happen in the next two years and underestimate what will happen in ten. I'm guilty of this myself" to 1996, The Road Ahead by Bill Gates with Nathan Myhrvold and Peter Rinearson, Second Edition, Section: Afterword, Quote Page 316, Penguin Books, New York.

Quote Investigator gives the earliest known appearance of the maxim as J. C. R. Licklider's Libraries of the Future (MIT Press, 1965), Chapter 1, page 17 — "A modern maxim says: 'People tend to overestimate what can be done in one year and to underestimate what can be done in five or ten years'" — with Licklider disclaiming authorship.

Quote Investigator cites Gates's later variant "we always overestimate the change that will occur in the next two years and underestimate the change that will occur in the next ten" to Business @ the Speed of Thought (1999), Chapter 4: Ride the Inflection Rocket, page 69, Warner Books, New York.

Quote Investigator concludes Roy Amara did not originate the saying, and its earliest Amara-linked citation is a 1983 Gannett News Service interview (with further 1989 and 1997 instances); it also finds the evidence linking Arthur C. Clarke to this specific expression weak, his 1951 statement being about daring prophecies seeming laughably conservative.

The WIST quotations database carries "People often overestimate what will happen in the next two years and underestimate what will happen in ten" cited to The Road Ahead, "Afterword" (1996 ed.), noting similar formulations circulating since the 1960s and linking to Quote Investigator.

The Road Ahead was first published by Viking Penguin on 24 November 1995 by Bill Gates with Nathan Myhrvold and Peter Rinearson; a revised paperback subtitled "Completely revised and up-to-date" was published by Penguin Books in October 1996, reflecting the internet's rapid rise after the hardback treated it as one important precursor to the information highway.

Bill Gates (William Henry Gates III) was born 28 October 1955, is American, co-founded Microsoft with Paul Allen in 1975, served as CEO for 25 years and later as chief software architect, and his books include The Road Ahead and Business @ the Speed of Thought.
Wikiquote's Bill Gates page does not list this line in any section (sourced, attributed or misattributed).
The Internet Archive holds an item catalogued as The Road Ahead by Gates, Bill, 1955–, publisher London: Penguin, dated 1996, originally published London: Viking, 1995.

Roy Charles Amara (7 April 1925 – 31 December 2007) was an American researcher and futurist, president of the Institute for the Future, whose name is attached to "Amara's law": "We tend to overestimate the effect of a technology in the short run and underestimate the effect in the long run."

J. C. R. Licklider (11 March 1915 – 26 June 1990) was an American psychologist and computer scientist who headed ARPA's Information Processing Techniques Office and wrote Libraries of the Future, published by MIT Press in 1965.
